title: OpenAI Responds to Apple’s Lawsuit and Motion for Preliminary Injunction: ‘Apple Is Getting This Wrong’
excerpt: A blog post is an unusual way to respond to a high-stakes lawsuit, but OpenAI is an unusual company. A few snippets from their post, and some commentary.
content_html:
OpenAI published an unbylined blog post overnight, responding in public — but not yet in court — to Apple’s new motion for a preliminary injunction. It’s an unusual move to respond to a high-stakes legal filing with a blog post, but OpenAI is an unusual company. A few snippets from their post, and some commentary:

Apple had claimed that they contacted OpenAI in February and that we didn’t respond. They now admit that their outside lawyers emailed the wrong person after confusing two Asian last names — only after we brought this to their attention.

OpenAI is hanging on to the fact that Apple’s outside counsel, Gabriel Gross, sent one email to the wrong address, and quickly emailed an apology. In OpenAI’s phrasing, it sounds like Apple’s attorney sent the entire initial letter of concern to the wrong person, and that’s why OpenAI never responded — because it wasn’t sent to the correct person (OpenAI general counsel Che Chang). That’s not what happened. The initial blockbuster “hey we think you guys are stealing our trade secrets and we want to talk to you about it” letter was sent to Che Chang. And Che Chang never did respond to Apple’s lawyers. That a mistaken email thanking Che Chang for a phone call that never happened (because that email was intended for another OpenAI employee) was also sent is irrelevant. I don’t understand why OpenAI is continuing to focus on this inconsequential mistake. (Apple’s motion for a preliminary injunction includes the full text of the mistaken email and subsequent apology.)

Apple accuses Chang Liu of accessing Apple confidential information after leaving the company, but only now admits that Apple employees reached out to him and asked for his help to locate this information (you can read the messages here). Apple now tries to shift the blame to “residual access”, but they also don’t disclose that this is a common issue with Apple which is caused by them failing to properly manage system access when people leave. What that means in practice is that former employees who are trying to do the right thing when they leave still have access to Apple files — despite not wanting them or even being aware of them.

OpenAI is seemingly alluding to Apple’s unusual use of iCloud Drive, tied to employees’ personal Apple Account IDs, that I (coincidentally?) wrote about yesterday. Apple’s motion for injunction, however, addresses this very point. From page 3 of the motion:

Mr. Liu resigned on Thursday, January 22, 2026, and provided notice that he would start at OpenAI the following Tuesday. On his last day, he failed to respond to Apple’s attempt to schedule his exit interview or sign his confidentiality reminder.

In the days following his departure, Mr. Liu seemed initially cooperative and aware of his obligations to Apple. He worked with others on his former Apple team to return certain Apple information remaining on his personal iCloud account to Apple.1 He also continued to converse with former co-workers, for example, to answer questions about his earlier work and where certain information was stored. But these interactions and exchanges cannot explain the repeated, unauthorized downloading of voluminous technical files from Apple’s cloud-based storage discussed below, which Mr. Liu performed on multiple occasions from February to April 2026 while employed by OpenAI.

That footnote reads:

1 While Apple seeks discovery into what Apple confidential information Mr. Liu accessed from his personal storage accounts (including iCloud) and devices after his departure, the specific unauthorized downloads referenced in the complaint and at the heart of this motion are not based on iCloud activity, but instead relate to Apple’s third-party cloud storage.

Nowhere in any of Apple’s filings (here’s the Court Listener index page for all the documents filed in the case) does it say who the third-party cloud storage provider is, but I’m almost certain it’s Box, which I know is widely used throughout Apple.

The iMessage transcripts that OpenAI provides at the bottom of their post do not contradict Apple’s claims at all. Apple’s motion states that Liu helped former colleagues find certain documents that were in iCloud; that’s what OpenAI’s transcript shows. But that’s not in dispute. Apple also claims that Liu accessed confidential information, presumably in Box and definitely not in iCloud Drive, on five different occasions, up until 27 April 2026, over three months after he left Apple. These chat transcripts offer no explanation for that. The chat transcripts explain iCloud Drive access that Apple itself says is not in dispute, and do not explain the 37 documents Liu downloaded from the third-party cloud provider (Box?) that Apple says are at the heart of naming him in the lawsuit. Here is Apple’s declaration from digital forensic specialist Daniel Roffman, documenting Liu’s access to confidential files post-employment (albeit with significant redactions).

I do not understand why OpenAI is treating this as a PR problem instead of as a legal problem. Dan Moren, linking to it from Six Colors, is of similar mind, writing:

What kept running through my head while reading this was the old legal chestnut: “If you have the facts on your side, pound the facts. If you have the law on your side, pound the law. If you have neither on your side, pound the table.”

Thus far this feels like table-pounding from OpenAI to me. Their blog post does, however, move the ball from “we have no interest” in Apple’s trade secrets to “we don’t have them”, (emphasis added):

Apple also accuses Tang Tan of trying to get and use their trade secrets. However, Tang has always been clear with the team that we do not want, and must not use, any confidential information from other companies. Tang served Apple for more than 24 years and was widely known as one of the most innovative leaders at the company. [...]

Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction is both based on false information and completely unnecessary because we do not have, nor want, any of their trade secrets. We’re much more interested in building innovative products and technologies that push the frontier.

To me, the most interesting response from OpenAI wasn’t their blog post. It was an email released by Apple, as “Exhibit F” to one of their expert declarations submitted to the court last night. OpenAI has retained the renowned law firm Quinn Emanuel as outside counsel, and this exhibit is a long email from Quinn Emanuel attorney Patrick Curran to Apple’s attorneys. From that email, dated Monday July 20, Curran writes:

You also ask that we “revisit” the specific points proposed in your July 15 letter. It appears that you want to move backwards. As noted, we already discussed these during our meet and confer but Apple was unable to respond to basic questions my colleagues raised about these requests. For example, your letter proposes that OpenAI “[p]roduce witnesses to testify at deposition” but Apple was unable to identify who those witnesses would be. Similarly, Apple was unsure when we asked if it was actually proposing that hundreds of OpenAI employees fill out “questionnaires” even if Apple has no basis to allege (and is indeed not alleging) that such employees have any connection to this litigation. The seven sections in your letter are broadly worded and remain vague and general. This is not what a forensic protocol looks like and we’re sure you understand that you will not get this as relief from the court. You first need to (preliminarily) identify the TS you are suing for, and your email states that you “appreciate the need” to do so. Any protocol will be informed by such identification. A forensic protocol cannot be based on general terms like “Apple confidential information”; you need to tell us what you’re looking for, and it sounds like you understand that and are prepared to do so. The efficient way forward is therefore to tackle these issues as part of the negotiation of a proper, detailed forensic protocol. If you instead prefer to move for a PI because OpenAI did not agree off the bat to subject hundreds of employees to “questionnaires” about “Apple confidential information” generally, that is unfortunate — and inconsistent with what I understand both our clients have requested. If you choose this path instead of working with us, we look forward to filing an opposition that sets the record straight.

Apple, obviously, did choose this path (“PI” = preliminary injunction), and I too look forward to OpenAI’s setting the record straight, especially if they do so in plainspoken language like Curran’s in this email. Curran continues:

Finally, although I know OpenAI would like to resolve this amicably, as their counsel I have to tell you what I think you already know — this case lacks merit. You have not articulated any basis to support a preliminary injunction. Your complaint is predicated on a misrepresentation of facts and allegations that are speculative at best. It fails to even remotely identify any trade secrets. You are attacking ordinary business practices (used widely across the industry). You are complaining about situations that you have caused, including through your own procedures and decisions. We stand ready to oppose any preliminary injunction motion and tell the world what really happened here to set the record straight. We made clear we would prefer to quickly and collaboratively address any legitimate concerns that your client has, but that is not well-served by repeated threats.

This email is a far better response than what OpenAI published on their blog.

blocks.html_en: The iMessage transcripts that OpenAI provides at the bottom of their post do not contradict Apple’s claims at all. Apple’s motion states that Liu helped former colleagues find certain documents that were in iCloud; that’s what OpenAI’s transcript shows. But that’s not in dispute. Apple also claims that Liu accessed confidential information, presumably in Box and definitely not in iCloud Drive, on five different occasions, up until 27 April 2026, over three months after he left Apple. These chat transcripts offer no explanation for that. The chat transcripts explain iCloud Drive access that Apple itself says is not in dispute, and do not explain the 37 documents Liu downloaded from the third-party cloud provider (Box?) that Apple says are at the heart of naming him in the lawsuit. Here is Apple’s declaration from digital forensic specialist Daniel Roffman, documenting Liu’s access to confidential files post-employment (albeit with significant redactions).

blocks.html_en: To me, the most interesting response from OpenAI wasn’t their blog post. It was an email released by Apple, as “Exhibit F” to one of their expert declarations submitted to the court last night. OpenAI has retained the renowned law firm Quinn Emanuel as outside counsel, and this exhibit is a long email from Quinn Emanuel attorney Patrick Curran to Apple’s attorneys. From that email, dated Monday July 20, Curran writes:

sentences.zh: 对我来说，OpenAI 最有趣的回应不是他们的博客文章。

sentences.en: It was an email released by Apple, as “Exhibit F” to one of their expert declarations submitted to the court last night.
sentences.zh: 这是苹果公司发布的一封电子邮件，作为昨晚向法院提交的一份专家声明的“证据 F”。

sentences.en: OpenAI has retained the renowned law firm Quinn Emanuel as outside counsel, and this exhibit is a long email from Quinn Emanuel attorney Patrick Curran to Apple’s attorneys.
sentences.zh: OpenAI 聘请了著名律师事务所 Quinn Emanuel 作为外部法律顾问，本展品是 Quinn Emanuel 律师 Patrick Curran 写给苹果律师的一封长电子邮件。

sentences.en: From that email, dated Monday July 20, Curran writes:
sentences.zh: 在 7 月 20 日星期一的电子邮件中，Curran 写道：

blocks.html_en: You also ask that we “revisit” the specific points proposed in your July 15 letter. It appears that you want to move backwards. As noted, we already discussed these during our meet and confer but Apple was unable to respond to basic questions my colleagues raised about these requests. For example, your letter proposes that OpenAI “[p]roduce witnesses to testify at deposition” but Apple was unable to identify who those witnesses would be. Similarly, Apple was unsure when we asked if it was actually proposing that hundreds of OpenAI employees fill out “questionnaires” even if Apple has no basis to allege (and is indeed not alleging) that such employees have any connection to this litigation. The seven sections in your letter are broadly worded and remain vague and general. This is not what a forensic protocol looks like and we’re sure you understand that you will not get this as relief from the court. You first need to (preliminarily) identify the TS you are suing for, and your email states that you “appreciate the need” to do so. Any protocol will be informed by such identification. A forensic protocol cannot be based on general terms like “Apple confidential information”; you need to tell us what you’re looking for, and it sounds like you understand that and are prepared to do so. The efficient way forward is therefore to tackle these issues as part of the negotiation of a proper, detailed forensic protocol. If you instead prefer to move for a PI because OpenAI did not agree off the bat to subject hundreds of employees to “questionnaires” about “Apple confidential information” generally, that is unfortunate — and inconsistent with what I understand both our clients have requested. If you choose this path instead of working with us, we look forward to filing an opposition that sets the record straight.

content_html_zh:
OpenAI 连夜发表了一篇未署名的博客文章，对苹果提出的初步禁令新动议进行了公开回应，但尚未在法庭上回应。 通过博客文章回应高风险的法律申请是一个不寻常的举动，但 OpenAI 是一家不寻常的公司。 他们的帖子中的一些片段以及一些评论：

苹果声称他们在 2 月份联系了 OpenAI，但我们没有做出回应。 他们现在承认，在我们提请他们注意此事之后，他们的外部律师在混淆了两个亚洲姓氏后向错误的人发送了电子邮件。

OpenAI 坚持认为，苹果公司的外部法律顾问加布里埃尔·格罗斯 (Gabriel Gross) 向错误的地址发送了一封电子邮件，并很快通过电子邮件道歉。 用 OpenAI 的措辞来说，听起来苹果的律师将整封最初的关注信发给了错误的人，这就是 OpenAI 从未回复的原因——因为它没有发送给正确的人（OpenAI 总法律顾问 Che Chang）。 事实并非如此。 最初的重磅信件“嘿，我们认为你们正在窃取我们的商业机密，我们想和你们谈谈这件事”，这封信是寄给 Che Chang 的。 而张澈也从未对苹果的律师做出回应。 一封错误的电子邮件感谢 Che Chang 打了一个从未打过的电话（因为该电子邮件是写给另一位 OpenAI 员工的），这也是无关紧要的。 我不明白为什么 OpenAI 继续关注这个无关紧要的错误。 （苹果公司提出的初步禁令动议包括错误电子邮件的全文以及随后的道歉。）

苹果指控刘畅在离开公司后访问了苹果的机密信息，但直到现在才承认苹果员工曾联系过他并请求他帮助查找这些信息（您可以在此处阅读这些消息）。 苹果现在试图将责任归咎于“剩余访问”，但他们也没有透露这是苹果的一个常见问题，这是由于他们未能在人们离开时正确管理系统访问而造成的。 这在实践中意味着，那些在离职后试图做正确事情的前员工仍然可以访问苹果文件——尽管他们不想要这些文件，甚至不知道这些文件。

OpenAI 似乎暗指苹果对 iCloud Drive 的不寻常使用，它与员工的个人 Apple 帐户 ID 绑定在一起，我（巧合？） 写了昨天的事。 然而，苹果公司的禁令动议正是解决了这一点。 议案第 3 页：

刘先生于 2026 年 1 月 22 日星期四辞职，并通知他将于下周二开始在 OpenAI 工作。 在他任职的最后一天，他没有回应苹果公司试图安排他的离职面谈或签署保密提醒的行为。 在他离开后的几天里，刘先生最初似乎很合作，并且意识到自己对苹果的义务。 他与前 Apple 团队的其他人合作，将其个人 iCloud 帐户中剩余的某些 Apple 信息归还给 Apple。1 他还继续与前同事交谈，例如回答有关他早期工作以及某些信息存储位置的问题。 但这些互动和交流无法解释下文讨论的从苹果云存储中重复、未经授权下载大量技术文件的行为，刘先生在 OpenAI 工作期间曾在 2026 年 2 月至 2026 年 4 月期间多次执行此操作。

该脚注如下：

1 虽然苹果公司寻求查明刘先生在离开后从他的个人存储帐户（包括 iCloud）和设备中访问了哪些苹果机密信息，但投诉中提到的特定未经授权的下载以及本动议的核心并非基于 iCloud 活动，而是与苹果的第三方云存储有关。

在苹果公司的任何文件中（这是该案提交的所有文件的法庭听众索引页）都没有提到第三方云存储提供商是谁，但我几乎可以肯定它是 Box，我知道它在整个苹果公司广泛使用。

OpenAI 在帖子底部提供的 iMessage 记录与苹果的说法完全不矛盾。 苹果公司的动议称，刘帮助前同事找到了 iCloud 中的某些文件；这就是 OpenAI 的记录所显示的内容。 但这是没有争议的。 苹果还声称，截至 2026 年 4 月 27 日，也就是他离开苹果三个多月后，刘在五个不同的场合访问了机密信息，可能是在 Box 中，而不是在 iCloud Drive 中。 这些聊天记录对此没有提供任何解释。 聊天记录解释了苹果自己所说的 iCloud Drive 访问不存在争议的情况，并且没有解释刘从第三方云提供商（Box？）下载的 37 个文件。 苹果公司表示，这是在诉讼中点名他的核心原因。 以下是苹果公司数字取证专家丹尼尔·罗夫曼 (Daniel Roffman) 的声明，记录了刘在离职后访问机密文件的情况（尽管进行了重大修改）。

我不明白为什么 OpenAI 将此视为公关问题而不是法律问题。 丹·莫伦（Dan Moren）在《六色》中链接到该文章，也有类似的想法，他写道：

读到这篇文章时，我脑子里一直萦绕着一个古老的法律栗子：“如果事实站在你这边，那就打击事实。 如果法律站在你这一边，那就遵守法律。 如果两者都不站在你这一边，那就拍桌子吧。”

到目前为止，这对我来说就像是 OpenAI 的重击。 然而，他们的博客文章确实将问题从“我们对苹果的商业秘密不感兴趣”转变为“我们没有它们”（强调）：

苹果还指控唐探试图获取和使用他们的商业机密。 然而，唐一直向团队明确表示，我们不希望、也决不能使用其他公司的任何机密信息。 唐在苹果公司工作了超过 24 年，被广泛认为是该公司最具创新精神的领导者之一。 [...] 苹果提出的初步禁令请求既基于虚假信息，也是完全没有必要的，因为我们没有也不想要他们的任何商业秘密。 我们对构建推动前沿的创新产品和技术更感兴趣。

对我来说，OpenAI 最有趣的回应不是他们的博客文章。 这是苹果公司发布的一封电子邮件，作为昨晚向法院提交的一份专家声明的“证据 F”。 OpenAI 聘请了著名律师事务所 Quinn Emanuel 作为外部法律顾问，本展品是 Quinn Emanuel 律师 Patrick Curran 写给苹果律师的一封长电子邮件。 在 7 月 20 日星期一的电子邮件中，Curran 写道：

您还要求我们“重新审视”您 7 月 15 日信中提出的具体要点。 看来你想向后退。 如前所述，我们已经在会议和会议期间讨论了这些问题，但苹果无法回应我的同事就这些请求提出的基本问题。 例如，您的信中建议 OpenAI“派出证人在作证时作证”，但苹果无法确定这些证人是谁。 同样，当我们询问苹果公司是否真的建议数百名 OpenAI 员工填写“调查问卷”时，苹果公司也不确定，即使苹果公司没有依据声称（而且确实没有声称）这些员工与这起诉讼有任何联系。 你信中的七个部分措辞宽泛，仍然模糊和笼统。 这不是法医协议的样子，我们确信您明白，您不会从法院获得此救济。 您首先需要（初步）确定您所起诉的 TS，并且您的电子邮件表明您“非常有必要”这样做。 任何协议都将通过此类标识来通知。 取证协议不能基于“Apple 机密信息”等笼统术语；您需要告诉我们您在寻找什么，听起来您了解这一点并准备这样做。 因此，有效的前进方法是在制定适当、详细的取证协议的谈判中解决这些问题。 如果你因为 OpenAI 不同意立即对数百名员工进行有关“Apple 机密信息”的“调查问卷”而更愿意跳槽成为 PI，那是不幸的，而且与我理解的我们客户的要求不一致。 如果您选择这条道路而不是与我们合作，我们期待提出异议以澄清事实。

显然，苹果确实选择了这条道路（“PI”=初步禁令），我也期待 OpenAI 澄清事实，特别是如果他们用像 Curran 在这封电子邮件中那样直白的语言这样做的话。 柯兰继续说道：

最后，虽然我知道 OpenAI 希望友好地解决这个问题，但作为他们的顾问，我必须告诉你我认为你已经知道的事情——这个案子缺乏优点。 您尚未阐明任何支持初步禁令的依据。 您的投诉是基于对事实的歪曲和指控，充其量只是推测。 它甚至无法远程识别任何商业秘密。 您正在攻击普通的商业实践（在整个行业中广泛使用）。 您正在抱怨您造成的情况，包括通过您自己的程序和决定造成的情况。 我们随时准备反对任何初步禁令动议，并告诉世界这里到底发生了什么，以澄清事实。 我们明确表示，我们希望快速、协作地解决您客户的任何合理担忧，但反复的威胁并不能很好地解决这一问题。

这封电子邮件的回复比 OpenAI 在其博客上发布的内容要好得多。
